title: Supervised learning
intro: Model, parameters, loss function, training and testing, illustrated with 1D linear regression.

questions.q: What roles do the model equation and the parameters ϕ play in y = f[x, ϕ]?
opts: The equation defines a family of possible relationships, and the parameters select a particular one
The equation is trained, and the parameters are fixed in advance
The parameters determine the form of the equation, for example linear or quadratic
Both are derived anew during training
questions.exp: In linear regression the family is the set of all lines. The y-intercept and slope determine the particular line.

opts: A scalar that summarizes how poorly the model with parameters ϕ predicts the training outputs
The deviation of the prediction for a single new example
The number of misclassified test examples
The difference between training and test performance
questions.exp: A small loss means a good fit to the training data. On its own, it says nothing about generalization.

questions.q: Why are the deviations squared in the least-squares loss?
opts: The direction of the deviation, above or below the data, should not matter. Theoretical reasons follow in chapter 5.
So that outliers receive less weight
So that the loss is linear in the parameters
So that the loss can always reach exactly zero
questions.exp: Without squaring, positive and negative deviations would cancel out. Note that squaring gives large deviations more weight, so it does not dampen outliers.

questions.q: In the heatmap of the loss function (figure 2.3), what does the minimum correspond to?
opts: The parameters of the best-fitting line
The line with the steepest slope
The point where the y-intercept is zero
The training example with the smallest error
questions.exp: Every point on the surface is a pair of parameters, and therefore a line. The lowest point belongs to the line with the smallest loss.

questions.q: How does the iterative training procedure described in the book work?
opts: Initialize randomly, measure the gradient at the current position, step in the direction of steepest descent, and repeat until the gradient is flat
Evaluate every combination of parameters and choose the best
Redraw the parameters at random until the loss falls below a threshold
Adjust the parameters to fit each training example exactly, one at a time
questions.exp: This is gradient descent. With two parameters an exhaustive evaluation is still feasible, with millions it is not.

questions.q: Linear regression has a closed-form solution. Why does the book still use gradient descent?
opts: More complex models have no closed-form solution and too many parameters to evaluate the loss for every combination
The closed-form solution is always numerically unstable
Gradient descent finds a better minimum for linear regression
The closed-form solution requires test data
questions.exp: The example introduces a procedure that becomes indispensable for deep networks later on.

questions.q: Why is the loss computed on a separate test set?
opts: To check how well the model generalizes to examples it did not observe during training
To fine-tune the parameters a second time
To confirm the training loss
To determine the learning rate
questions.exp: A small training loss only shows a good fit to known data. Only the test shows whether the model is ready to deploy.

questions.q: According to the book, what determines how well prediction accuracy generalizes to test data?
opts: How representative and complete the training data is, and how expressive the model is
Only the number of training iterations
Only the size of the test set
The choice of initial parameters
questions.exp: Both factors interact. Even the best model cannot compensate for situations that are missing from the training data.

opts: A very expressive model describes statistical peculiarities of the training data that are atypical, leading to unusual predictions
The model has a training loss that is too large
The model is too simple for the data
The training data contains too many features
questions.exp: Overfitting typically shows up as a low training loss combined with a much higher test loss.

questions.q: How does a generative model x = g[y, ϕ] differ from a discriminative model y = f[x, ϕ]?
opts: It computes the measurements from the output. To make a prediction, it has to be inverted, which may be difficult.
It does not need training data
It always returns probabilities instead of point estimates
It can only be used for images
questions.exp: Discriminative models predict y directly from x. Generative models describe how the data x is created from y.

questions.q: A model that predicts order lead times achieves a very low training loss but makes large errors on new orders. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Overfitting: the model learned peculiarities of the historical orders that do not generalize
Underfitting: the model is too simple
Gradient descent has not converged
The loss function is wrong because it squares the errors
questions.exp: Low training loss and high test loss is the typical pattern. It is also worth checking how representative the data is, for example with new product variants, and how expressive the model is.

questions.q: An energy model of a press uses a single straight line over the stroke rate. Both training and test error are high. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Underfitting: the model family is too restricted to capture the actual relationship
Overfitting to the training data
Too little test data
The parameters were initialized badly
questions.exp: If the model cannot even explain the training data well, it lacks expressiveness. The shallow neural networks in chapter 3 describe a much larger family of functions.

questions.q: An energy baseline for a machine was trained and tested on data from the summer months. The test error is low. In winter, the predictions deviate strongly. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The training data does not represent the winter operating conditions, and the test set shares the same gap
Overfitting, because the model learned peculiarities of individual summer days
Underfitting, because the model family is too restricted for the relationship
Gradient descent stopped before reaching the minimum of the loss
questions.exp: The low test error rules out a pure overfitting or underfitting problem on the observed conditions. A test set only measures generalization within the conditions it covers. Winter lies outside, so the training data needs to include it.
